title: From the dear, grief (209–216)
hookLine: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one free of it has neither

lines: A STRANGER'S PHONE IN THE LAKE.
WHAT WE LOVE CAN HURT US.
cards: A stranger's phone falls in a lake, and nobody loses sleep. A coworker's cousin has surgery, and the day goes on. But a parent's kid is ten minutes late, and the stomach starts to knot.

A dog limps, and the whole evening goes gray. The things we love are exactly the things that can hurt us, and still, people go on loving. Chapter sixteen of the Dhammapada looks at that trade with unusual honesty.

teach.b: Chapter sixteen is called Piyavagga. Piya means dear, beloved, precious; Müller titled it pleasure, but dear is closer.

Verse two twelve, in his words: "From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear." In Pali: from what is dear comes sorrow, from what is dear comes fear.
The next four verses repeat it with other words: from affection, from lust, from love, from craving.
Five times, the same shape. There's a story in the Udāna, one of the early collections.

Visākhā, a devoted lay follower of the Buddha, came to him in wet clothes and wet hair, grieving a grandchild who had died. He asked her: would you like as many children and grandchildren as there are people in this city?
Yes, she said. And how many people die in this city each day? Many, she said.
Then, he answered gently, you'd never be without wet clothes and wet hair. Those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have none have none.
This is hard teaching, and verse two eleven goes further, in Müller's words: "Let, therefore, no man love anything; loss of the beloved is evil." Buddhists read that in more than one way.
Some take it strictly, as monastics do when they leave close family ties behind.
Some teachers read it as being about grasping: love fully, hold loosely, knowing that everything dear will change.
The tradition's own loving-kindness, metta, wishes all beings well without clutching any of them. Either way, the verses tell the truth about love's cost.

how: Buddhist monastics leave close family ties behind, and some teachers present these verses to lay people as a call to love without clinging, and to meet loss with the understanding that everything dear will change.

o: a vow you make to a teacher
the grief that follows a loss

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.

s: verses 212 to 216 repeat one shape with five different words
pleasure, affection, lust, love and greed, in Müller's English.
Buddhists all read these verses the same way
some read them strictly; some teachers read them as being about grasping.
Müller's 'pleasure' translates piya, which means dear
from what is dear comes grief.

games.q: you're Visākhā, grieving a grandchild. the Buddha asks: would you like as many children and grandchildren as there are people in this city? what do you say?
games.why: she said yes. then he asked how many die there each day: many. "you'd never be without wet clothes and wet hair."

practice: Bring to mind one person, animal or thing you love, and feel the love warmly, fully.

Then notice whether there's a small grip in it too, a fear of losing it, and soften that grip the way you'd open a fist that was holding a bird too tightly. Wish them well: may you be safe, may you be at ease, whatever happens.

wordCard.voice: Piya. Dear, beloved, precious: verse two twelve says from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one who is free of it knows neither.

orig.note: Pali: dear, beloved — piyato jāyatī soko, from the dear arises sorrow.

carryVoice: Your line: love fully, hold loosely. Wish them well without clutching any of them. That's one ninety-nine.
